Nongrum has taten pains to compile a compendium of Khasi papers and Khasi books with a view to providing a coherent and developing account of the tradition of Khasi literature. The book cannot, however, be treated as a literary survey descri- bing the general characteristics of the period’s literature in such a way as enabling the reader to trace its growth and keep his bearings. The book does not provide an account of contemporary society at its points of contact with literature. The first section of the Book deals with the Khasi papers dating back to 1889 which year the first Khasi paper entitled *U Nongkitkhubor* and edited by Rev. William Williams appeared in print. It was written from a Christian angle but it contained articles on Khasi religion, marriage feast

according to Khasi society and culture. The Khasi poem "U Sirlapalang’ in 51 stanzas composed by Rev. Morkha Joseph Chyne, the Khasi poet, was published in this paper. Between 1889 and 1980 eighty six Khasi papers were added. Some of these articles were written in literary style and had rich literary contents. The khasi papers were arranged in a chronological order containing the main objectives. This type of compila- tion stimulates the spent of enquiry and research. Such questions may be raised - What was the reaction between writer and public? What was the reading public like in its tastes and make up? How many survive to this day? Is it dearth of creative writens, lack of training, paucity of reading public? The second section deals with the list of Khasi books. The hills and vales of Khasi Hills were full of Khasi folk lores, tales of heroism etc and these were woven round the fire-place and transmitted by word of mouth from one generation to another, but these were lost in oblivion for lack of writing medium. The Khasi alphabets in Roman form come rather too late. It was Rev. Thomas Jones, the pathfinder, who invented the khasi alphabets and offered a suitable medium for expression of Khasi thought] The first Khasi books which appeared in print were written in archaic style but with passing of time many changes in spelling and accent were introduce like the original *c* changed to 'k* The books are arrange starting with the name of the author and not in a chronological order. Literature is to be viewed not as a mere academic product but as one expression of the many - sided activities of national growth, historical sketch of contemporary social and political events as a prelude to every important period in the deve- lopment of any literature. The various stages of literary development are absent for lack of a proper chronology. In any anthology not all the books are included. There is a tesk of selection to be performed based on works which are of more value than others keeping in

view the function of criticism which in old days was neither respected nor competently performed. Yet on the whole the compilation is to be highly commended. •‘KI KOT KHUBOR KHASI BAD KI KOT KHHSI” 

by u Kitbor W. Nongrum. 

A Fore ward by Rev J.L. Roy. 

The author, u Kitbor W. Nongrum has taten pains to 
compile a compendium of Khasi papers and Khasi books 
with a view to providing a coherent and developing 
account of the tradition of Khasi literature. The book 
cannot, however, be treated as a literary survey descri- 
bing the general characteristics of the period’s literature 
in such a way as enabling the reader to trace its growth 
and keep his bearings. The book does not provide an 
account of contemporary society at its points of contact 
with literature. 

The first section of the Book deals with the Khasi 
papers dating back to 1889 which year the first Khasi paper 
entitled *U Nongkitkhubor* and edited by Rev. William 
Williams appeared in print. It was written from a Christian 
angle but it contained articles on Khasi religion, marriage 
feast according to Khasi society and culture. The Khasi 
poem "U Sirlapalang’ in 51 stanzas composed by Rev. 
Morkha Joseph Chyne, the Khasi poet, was published 
in this paper. Between 1889 and 1980 eighty six Khasi 
papers were added. Some of these articles were written in 
literary style and had rich literary contents. 

The khasi papers were arranged in a chronological 
order containing the main objectives. This type of compila- 
tion stimulates the spent of enquiry and research. Such 
questions may be raised - What was the reaction between 
writer and public? What was the reading public like in its 
tastes and make up? How many survive to this day? Is it 
dearth of creative writens, lack of training, paucity of 
reading public? 

The second section deals with the list of Khasi books. 
The hills and vales of Khasi Hills were full of Khasi folk 
lores, tales of heroism etc and these were woven round 
the fire-place and transmitted by word of mouth from one 
generation to another, but these were lost in oblivion for 
lack of writing medium. The Khasi alphabets in Roman 
form come rather too late. It was Rev. Thomas Jones, the 



pathfinder, who invented the khasi alphabets and offered 
a suitable medium for expression of Khasi thought] The 
first Khasi books which appeared in print were written in 
archaic style but with passing of time many changes in 
spelling and accent were introduce like the original *c* 
changed to 'k* 

The books are arrange starting with the name of the 
author and not in a chronological order. Literature is to 
be viewed not as a mere academic product but as one 
expression of the many - sided activities of national growth, 
historical sketch of contemporary social and political 
events as a prelude to every important period in the deve- 
lopment of any literature. The various stages of literary 
development are absent for lack of a proper chronology. 
In any anthology not all the books are included. There is 
a tesk of selection to be performed based on works which 
are of more value than others keeping in view the function 
of criticism which in old days was neither respected nor 
competently performed. 

Yet on the whole the compilation is to be highly 
commended.
